question: Did Pātañjala Yoga take its shared meditative and ethical vocabulary (the four attitudes, the five faculties, the afflictions, samāpatti, dharmamegha) from Buddhism, or do Yoga, Buddhism and Jainism draw on a common śramaṇa milieu?

sides.position: Yoga is an ancient teaching (the tradition names Hiraṇyagarbha as its first teacher and Patañjali as its compiler); the Yoga text marks its difference from the Buddhists, rejecting the view that objects are constructions of a single mind; no dependence on Buddhism is acknowledged.
arguments: one object is shared by many minds and does not depend on a single mind (YS 4.15–16)
the bhāṣya states and refutes the idealist argument (YBh 4.14)

sides.position: The suttas themselves acknowledge that other wanderers taught the abandoning of the hindrances and the four immeasurables, and that the bodhisatta learned the formless attainments from other teachers; the Buddha's distinctiveness lies in knowing where these culminate and in the liberating insight beyond them.
arguments: each liberation of mind has a stated culmination only the Tathāgata can explain (SN 46.54)
the formless attainments learned from Āḷāra and Uddaka were judged insufficient (MN 26)

sides.position: The five great vows and the four reflections belong to the Jina's teaching; Haribhadra treats the yoga taught by others as one path of qualities under different names, correlating his eight views with the limbs beginning with yama.
arguments: the five vows and the name mahāvrata (TS 7.1–2)
the four reflections toward classes of beings (TS 7.11)
the eight views correlated with the eight limbs (YDS 16)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a historical question on which the traditions' own accounts and the scholarly hypotheses differ; no principle settles history.
candidate_readings: Common milieu: the object-class form of the four attitudes (YS 1.33 = TS 7.11, unlike the Pali formula) and the shared five vows suggest a common śramaṇa stock rather than one-way borrowing.
Specific borrowing: technical terms of Buddhist Abhidharma (anuśaya, the burnt seed, dharmamegha as a ground-name) may have been taken over by the Yoga authors (scholarly hypothesis).
P2-standpoint (doctrinal content only): the same practices described from different standpoints — boundless pervasion (Buddhist) versus attitudes suited to classes of beings (Yoga, Jain).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Yoga tradition does not acknowledge dependence on Buddhism; the Buddhist tradition claims its path differs in culmination; the Jain tradition derives its vows from the Jinas.

notes: Borrowing evidence: brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes, brw:buddhism-yoga-five-faculties, brw:buddhism-yoga-klesa-theory, brw:buddhism-yoga-meditation-vocabulary, brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha, brw:jain-four-bhavanas-and-yoga, brw:jain-mahavratas-and-yoga-yamas, brw:four-immeasurables-sramana-common, brw:yoga-refutes-buddhist-idealism.

question: How is another family's revelation to be placed — as a lower stage of one's own, as a deliberate delusion, as a subdued power, or as a partial standpoint?

sides.position: All philosophies are roles of the one conscious Lord: the Buddhists rest in the intellect-principle, the Jains in the qualities, the Vedic knowers in the Person, the Pāñcarātrikas in the unmanifest; the Trika alone knows the self as both transcendent and immanent.
Maheśvara and the worldly gods are subdued by Vajrapāṇi and given places in the Buddha's maṇḍala; they are worldly powers, not the goal.
The Buddha and the naked ascetics' teachers are Viṣṇu's deluding descent, sent to lead the enemies of the gods away from the Veda.
Every other doctrine is a one-sided standpoint; the Jina's word is the aggregate of all the wrong views, each true only when joined with the others.
Whatever is acceptable in the Vedāntins' teaching is acceptable only as the emptiness the Buddha taught.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each tradition applies stage and standpoint to the others while rejecting its own subordination.
candidate_readings: P4-stage and P2-standpoint applied symmetrically: every ranking is made from within one tradition's standpoint, so the rankings do not conflict as descriptions of their authors' own maps.
Record as mutual subordination and leave unreconciled, since each tradition's final goal is defined against the others.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Every tradition named rejects being placed below the others; the Jain many-sidedness itself claims to be the complete view.

question: Was haṭha yoga taught by Śiva (Ādinātha) through the Nāth siddhas, or did its earliest methods arise in a Buddhist tantric milieu?

sides.position: Haṭha was taught by Śrī Ādinātha (Śiva) and known by Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the other great siddhas, from whom Svātmārāma received it.
The Tibetan canon places the Amṛtasiddhi among the siddhas' works, opening with homage to Heruka and ascribed to the great master Virūpa.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a question of origins on which the two traditions' accounts differ.
candidate_readings: Several strands: a Buddhist-milieu bindu yoga (Amṛtasiddhi) and Śaiva/Kaula kuṇḍalinī and khecarī strands, joined in the later haṭha compilations (scholarly account).
A shared siddha milieu in which the same names (Virūpa/Virūpākṣa, Mīna, Cauraṅgī) belong to both traditions (see cpt:siddha-identifications).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The haṭha and Nāth traditions name Ādinātha as the source; the Tibetan tradition names Virūpa; neither refers to the other's account.
